'''American Empire''' was a geopolitical text putting forth the notion that, due to the Flood, the United States has become an "unintentional empire" and must start behaving in a more mature fashion befitting of such a nation.

==Overview==
==='''Part 1: The Origins of Empire'''===
The book was published while Stephen Michaels was president of the US Naval War College, and was a culmination of his ideas regarding US foreign policy and international relations.

Michaels began the book with an examination of what factors lead to America's economic power and geography's impact on a nation's foreign policy, focusing a great deal on how the country's rise to prominence after World War II. He identifies such features as geography, population, and government, and argues that American military supremacy is a consequence of these factors, reinforcing the belief in an "Unintentional Empire."

The book goes on to describe the power vacuum left after the fall of the Soviet Union and what the period of conflicts in the Middle East reveal about America's political immaturity.

==='''Part 2: Reconciling the Empire and the Republic'''===
The book's second section outlines the risk that the Empire plays to the Republican experiment, though makes few political assertions. Michaels instead focuses on historical examples of Republicans that fell to Imperialism. He asserts that the risk for the US is not the slow surrender of legislative authority the the President but rather the rise of a Caesar in response to political discord and corruption at the Federal Level.

==='''Part 3: The Necessary Doctrine'''===
The book's final chapter outwardly advocates for the next President to adopt a doctrine of local balance of power enabled by American military "Viceroys" who would command not only American troops, but have direct command over local forces; abandoning the alliance system of NATO in favor of more direct dominion. However, Michaels also argues that the US should reduce its permanent presence around the world in favor of a tiered system of priorities and deployments.

*Tier 1: Diplomatic relations
*Tier 2: Pressuring regional powers
*Tier 3: Balance of power
*Tier 4: Military cooperation
*Tier 5: Direct Intervention

==Impact on US foreign policy==

'''A State of Merit,''' is the 2039 magnum opus of American sociologist Brandon Tran. It created a profound shift in conservative politics, and formed the political manifesto of many post-flood policies that would define the early identity [[Conservative Party (United States)|Conservative Party]] of the United States. 

Eventually, its ideals out of many others had gradually helped and defined the rise of Neo-Jeffersonianism. Tran believed in limited regulations within business to help them expand employment, and argued that new automation technologies made the city preeminent over the state and nation-government by allowing solutions to problems to be rapidly tested and disseminated through society.

==Tran's aims in State of Merit==
Tran was a long time critic of many contemporary democratic institutions. He wrote that the current democratic system of the United states had devolved into a ‘popularity contest’ that can easily sway the masses to vote on whoever is more “good-looking, more confident, or already popular” the person is rather than how good a person are at his/her job. 

With multiple parties comes division with each side vying for control. He argued that each person of their own respective parties would identify and exaggerate many problems at hand to “forward their own agendas” and gather votes. And if such person loses an election, citizens of their party would cause violence within the streets costing lives and property damage in millions of dollars, citing the aftermath of the 2016 and the 2024 election. He argues that many current parts about democracy, specifically elections, promotes violent tendencies of citizens. He compares national/state elections to a game of sports; where two or more teams root for each other, if the game is hyped up enough and one side wins, the other losing side riots. (But he does accept this was what things were and what he should work with).

==Summary of the State of Merit==
==='''Part I: Introduction'''===
The first part of A State of Merit attempts to analyze the causes of the [[Great Reset]] and predicts the breakdown of the economic model established under the [[Dylan J. Price|Price administration]]. Tran supports the argument that the Great Reset was the inevitable result of the consolidation of power in the hands of a few major corporations, and even argues that the Progressives were right to carry out a new era of Trust Busting. He goes on to argue that the decision to nationalize larges segments of the economy was where the Price coalition went too far, and that it would inevitably lead to an economy that would be too inflexible to adapt to new technologies and social conditions.

==='''Part II: Definitions and ideas'''===
Tran advocates for the establishment of a purely meritorious system, devoid of human meddling and bias, which he argued was more achievable now with advanced automation technologies. He puts for the notion that automation has made it possible to distribute economic power more uniformly than at any point in human history, and that the government should support this effort with policies designed to encourage small businesses that can use new automation solutions to manage the workforce in a decentralized fashion .

And systems of smaller entities where it bases you on if you “work smart, not hard” whilst in line with laws and regulations. He believes that the more efficient and more resourceful you work, the more you should be rewarded (although it doesn’t mean that those who work hard wouldn’t get rewarded at all).

==='''Part III: The Inevitability of Patronage'''===
==='''Part IV: The Essential need of Meritocracy'''===

'''Tanning the Donkey: The Life and Death of the Democratic Party''' was created ten years in response to 'Skinning the Elephant', the book 
describes the series of circumstances that led to the rise of competing 
factions and the ultimate fracturing of the Democrat party after the 
fall of the Republican party. The book describes the Clinton Era to the 
last pitch of Julian Castro in 2032.

'''The Great Deluge '''was a''' '''scientific and sociological analysis of the Flood ending with several proposals of various solutions. Many of these proposals would go on to be the basis of several goals of the Earth Working Group. The term 'Great Deluge' was also popularized by the book.

'''Starbound''' describes the invention and evolution of early Terran space travel along with several scenarios and short stories of possible events leading up to and the results from its invention. It was influential to the creation of one of the first versions of the space warp drive.
[[Category:Literature]]

'''''Inevitable Tetrapods '''''was a composition of various theories attempting to explain the convergent evolution of tetrapod-esque (four-limbed) body plans on planets with complex animal-like life. The book's title is something of a misnomer, as it does acknowledge the existence of alien species with more than four limbs. Its main thesis, however, is that the evolution of four limbs is a "path of least resistance" for vertebrate-like organisms evolving a land-dwelling lifestyle, at least under Earth-like circumstances. The fewer limbs an organism has, so the argument goes, the less complex its movement, ergo the fewer resources it needs to consume.

Furthermore, the majority of land vertebrate-analogs on alien worlds were, like tetrapods on Earth, descended from fish-like swimmers (though they in turn often had ancestors that varied considerably--the first "vertebrates" on [[Tu]], for example, resembled velvet worms, but these later evolved a fishlike form). The fluidity of water, rather than other environmental conditions such as atmosphere composition or gravity, dictates the form of a swimming creature, so these swimmers often ended up looking superficially similar to fish on Earth, with torpedo-shaped bodies and fins. Such body shapes, the writers argued, were predisposed to evolving tetrapod-like forms when colonizing land.

Non-tetrapodal aliens, such as the [[Velminyak]], the [[Tel-bn]], and the [[Constructors]], seem to have primarily evolved on worlds where the common ancestor of the local land "vertebrates" were not fish-like. The Tel-bn evolved from amphibious squid-like creatures, the Velminyak from something akin to polychaetes, and the Constructors from creatures resembling starfish.

The book was well-received in the exobiological community, with biologist Lauren Naish going as far as to declare it "the best treatise ever written on convergent evolution and the forces that drive it," and calling it "a must-have for any lover of tetrapod zoology."
